It's not hard to understand that. It's that horror sells tickets to movies. There are plenty of books about one thing, but second-layer elements are better suited for the entertainment industry. An author can write whatever they want, it doesn't cost them anything to write a book, and to let a publisher decide if it's worth publishing. But it costs tens of millions of dollars to make a movie, so you have to earn that money back. And horror sells.

Also, I think that if a studio (this more about studios than directors) makes a more human-focused feature film based on King, they're in a tough spot as to marketing. You want to market that it's based on King, because that sells tickets. But most people think of King as horror (since more people go to movies than read books) and if they get a human story, they might be disappointed, and there goes your all-important rotten tomatoes score.

Novels also have to have 97% of the book cut out to fit into a movie. So what do you cut out? Short stories are better-suited, as everyone knows. A miniseries could do more to bring in the human element. Stand By Me is a great example of taking short story and focusing almost entirely on the human element. 

I'll have to check out Salem's Lot. That story really needs to be 7-10 hours though. I think studios basically just want to make horror movies (because they sell tickets) and if they can "base" it on Stephen King, all the better. But in some cases it's sort of window dressing.

I'm not suggesting King isn't horror, it's all about horror. But the cheap monster scare tactics aren't why King's works are so popular. Put the scares in, but make sure they come from the right source (people's inborn fears) and the horror takes on a new level of concern. Thus when Pennywise is shown on screen, about to eat a child, we have an emotional investment in that child (or at the very least the PTSD from his brother's guilt). Then it's not just about a scary clown showing up in a sewer because...money.

> the cheap monster scare tactics aren't why King's works are so popular

Right. He's a popular novelist. But books and movies are incredibly different mediums, and even more than that, are incredibly different industries. It's not about art, it's about commerce. When art happens in film, it's because (a) someone talented worked outside the system with micro budgets and independent financing, or (b) someone talented got lucky within the system, or (c) someone is so powerful that they get to do passion projects. 

The problem is King's name is associated with horror with most people, rather than human stories. Take two books, pretend there's generic author X and King. And they each write a book that's a story with horror as an element but human elements as the foundation. You usually can't fit enough of either in 110 minutes. You make Author X's story about the human elements, and King's about the horror. Because that's business. Not doing that is like not making french fries salty in fast food, or not making a jacket warm. 

It's also possible that early drafts of screenplays are ripe with human elements, and as the studio and marketing get involved, it slowly but surely replaces those elements with more and more horror. To continue the food metphor, horror is like cheese in the industry. You don't want to skimp on the cheese, you want to pile it on. So what if you overpower the olives—the only healthy part of the pizza anyway.

I get what you are saying, but it's all done because it has to make money. Not because people don't understand King's novels. And why King's novels should be made into miniseries, not films, they are too long and too rich for the restrictions of a movie's runtime.

You do have a point.

In the almost half-century of Stephen King on film, there has been no shortage of disappointing adaptations. (King himself deserves some blame for this -- *Maximum Overdrive*, *Sleepwalker*, the TV *The Shining,* etc.)

There have been dozens of subpar low-budget horror movies made from Stephen King novels and stories, for instance, like all the *Children of the Corn* sequels. There have been well-funded Stephen King disappointments like *The Dark Tower*, which failed to create a franchise. 

At the same time, however, there have been a lot of good-to-excellent adaptations.

You mention Darabont, Flanagan and Jason Bateman. Of course we need to add Rob Reiner to that list. I think we also need to add Brian De Palma -- *Carrie* is the movie that jumpstarted the Stephen King cinematic universe and has a very relatable human story at its core. George Romero is another name to add. *Creepshow*, written by King himself, is probably the best cinematic representation of King's dark humor and his *Twilight Zone*/pulp horror roots. (And is one of the very best comic book movies at looking and feeling like a comic book come to life.) *The Running Man*, directed by relatively unknown Paul Michael Glaser, is another decent cinematic adaptation of the pulp/dark comedy side of King.

I don't think it's a great film but *Christine*, directed by John Carpenter in his prime, is a movie that captures -- to some extent -- the Stephen King who chronicles the joys and pains of adolescence. 

And of course Stanley Kubrick directed THE Stephen King adaptation, a film that regardless of King's own complaints has become a cinematic classic. 

So I think you are underestimating the number of quality Stephen King adaptations: that capture something of his work beyond the ghosts and monsters. They're definitely out there.

> Are the filmmakers not responsible tho?

Depends on the situation. Very few filmmakers are powerful enough to call the shots totally. Studios have come in and saved many movies from directors, and studios have come in and ruined just as many. 

Ultimately, directors have to work. If their choice is between a lukewarm script and no work at all, they're going to do what they can with the script. And nobody ever knows if a movie will be good or not while it's being made. 

> But the cheap monster scare tactics aren't why King's works are so popular. 

He writes books. Those don't work in books. They work in movies. It's like asking why Burger King doesn't sell more salads than burgers, since salads are obviously better for you.

King is a tough guy to adapt for a variety of reasons. The first being that his most popular works are horror. Horror films are easy money for studios and King was a cultural phenomenon, so they tended to push them out quickly and hire cheap directors to maximize profit. So you’ve got a lot of lesser and/or inexperienced artists trying to cheaply adapt his bukkake style storytelling. Which leads into the second problem, and that’s that King overstuffed a lot of his books with bizarre plot lines that didn’t cleanly tie into the main story. It’s part of his charm and can make for an interesting read, put when adapting into film it’s tough to distill it into a cohesive story. It’s a catch-22; if you leave out the wacky shit in his books, you’re cutting out what makes his writing distinct. If you leave it in, your movie is probably going to have a messy narrative. 

I don’t think it’s an accident that a lot of the best adaptations are from talented filmmakers and feature his more “serious” works, short stories, and simpler narratives. Darabont’s three excellent adaptations are all from novellas. Same for Stand By Me, 1922, and Secret Window. Christine, Dolores Claiborne, Carrie, Misery, and Gerald’s Game are relatively concise stories. The first IT remake has all the best elements from the book (chapter two not so much), and Kubrick’s The Shining just uses the bones of the story. I think those all range from good to amazing. Dr. Sleep is the only one I can think of that functions despite how overstuffed and weird it is.
What do you think about King’s work as a screenwriter? He’s no stranger to adapting his own work for the big and small screen.

I came here to point this stuff out and flip the question a bit:

Why does Hollywood keep making Stephen King films?

There are so very many bad movies that his name should be box-office poison. To Stephen King fans, his name IS box-office poison because decades of bitter experience means that nine out of ten times the only reason to watch is to see how bad it is. I'm not even talking about bad adaptations here, I'm talking straight-up objectively bad movies.

There's some weird Hollywood-logic going on here because it's incredibly ironic when you think about it. 

The real reason King's name isn't box office poison is because most of his movies are so bad that hardly anyone has heard of, let alone seen, them. They HAVE seen stuff like Shawshank and know he's a best-selling author so, unlike Stephen King fans, they get their name recognition from that instead of the litany of bad movies and TV shows.

Thanks for not raking me over the coals. I'm not popular with Kubrick groupies (Kubrickies? lol) Clayborne was good. Mostly drama, not my jam but I will say it had the King undercurrent flowing. Posting tonight really got me to thinking about casting in King's adaptations...Gary Sinise in The Stand, Dr. Sleep cast, Kathy Bates so good in Clayborne & Misery, Sissy Spacek in Carrie...you mentioned Gwynne. It helps to have actors that have a firm grasp on material.

Because he’s one of the most popular and successful writers ever. That’s a pretty obvious answer. He appeals to both his devoted fans and the most casual of readers. He has star power. He is, to some extent, bankable. Any movie adaptation is going to get a certain amount of attention just because of his name attached to it.
